name: Question 18
problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=y(x+2),\,y(-1)=2
$$

Use the modified Euler method with one step to approximate $y(0).$

$y(0)≈$
{{field-1}}
worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the modified Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the initially predicted slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=0-(-1)=1.
$$

First, we add the initial condition data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, we compute the value of ${y}^{′}$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(x+2) \\  & =2(-1+2) \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $2$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =2\cdot 1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $2$ |  |  |  |

The coordinates of the initially predicted new point given by the predictor equation are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=-1+1=0, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=2+2=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $2$ | $4$ |  |  |

So, the predicted slope at this point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={y}_{p}({x}_{\text{new}}+2) \\  & =4(0+2) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{p}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2+8)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $5$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=0.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy=2+5=7
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $2$ | $4$ | $8$ | $5$ |
| $0$ | $7$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(0)≈7.$

−1 2 2 2

The coordinates of the initially predicted new point given by the predictor equation are xnew=x+Δx=−1+1=0,yp=y+Δyp=2+2=4.

−1 2 2 2 4

So, the predicted slope at this point is yp′=yp(xnew+2)=4(0+2)=8.

We can add this to our table.

−1 2 2 2 4 8

Finally, we compute Δy using the corrector equation: Δy=12(y′+yp′)⋅Δx=12(2+8)⋅1=12⋅10=5

x y y′ Δyp yp yp′ Δy
−1 2 2 2 4 8 5

x y y′ Δyp yp yp′ Δy

0 7
